clinicalPearls: A localised redundancy of the interatrial septum, usually at the fossa ovalis, that bulges and oscillates between the atria through the cardiac cycle
Defined echocardiographically by the excursion and base width of the mobile septal segment
Usually an incidental finding but clinically important because of its strong association with a patent foramen ovale and other interatrial communications
The combination of an atrial septal aneurysm and a patent foramen ovale raises the likelihood of paradoxical embolism and cryptogenic stroke compared with either alone
May act as a source of thrombus and is associated with atrial arrhythmias in some patients
Best characterised by transoesophageal echocardiography with an agitated-saline bubble study to demonstrate any accompanying shunt
Management is guided by the associated shunt and any embolic events; device closure may be considered when a high-risk PFO with aneurysm underlies a cryptogenic stroke
reference.pathophysiology: An atrial septal aneurysm is an area of thin, redundant tissue in the interatrial septum, typically involving the region of the fossa ovalis, that billows back and forth with the changing pressure gradient between the two atria. The increased mobility of the septum is frequently accompanied by incomplete sealing of the foramen ovale or by fenestrations, providing a route for right-to-left shunting when right atrial pressure transiently exceeds left. Stasis and the abnormal, mobile surface may promote local thrombus formation, and together with an associated patent foramen ovale this underlies the heightened risk of paradoxical systemic embolism.
additionalDifferentials: Lipomatous hypertrophy of the atrial septum
Atrial septal mass, thrombus, or tumour
Cor triatriatum or other atrial membrane
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography to detect septal bulging and measure its excursion
Transoesophageal echocardiography to define the aneurysm and any associated shunt or fenestrations
Agitated-saline bubble study with Valsalva to demonstrate right-to-left shunting
Cardiac MRI or CT to distinguish an aneurysm from lipomatous hypertrophy or a mass
Prolonged rhythm monitoring and embolic-source workup when stroke has occurred
redFlags: Cryptogenic stroke or systemic embolism, particularly with a coexisting patent foramen ovale
Demonstrable thrombus adherent to the aneurysmal septum
Recurrent embolic events despite antithrombotic treatment
A large right-to-left shunt provoked by Valsalva in the context of unexplained stroke
reference.prognosis: In isolation an atrial septal aneurysm is generally benign, but when combined with a patent foramen ovale it markedly increases the risk of paradoxical embolism and recurrent cryptogenic stroke, which appropriate treatment can reduce.
pitfalls: Reporting the aneurysm without actively searching for an associated shunt with a bubble study
Confusing the finding with lipomatous septal hypertrophy or an atrial mass
Missing the raised stroke risk conferred by the aneurysm-plus-PFO combination
Attributing stroke to the aneurysm before excluding atrial fibrillation and other embolic sources
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC Guidelines for the management of adult congenital heart disease
management: Reassure and observe an isolated atrial septal aneurysm, which is generally benign and needs no specific intervention

When associated with a patent foramen ovale and cryptogenic stroke, provide secondary prevention with antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy and consider percutaneous device closure of the patent foramen ovale
Undertake a thorough embolic-source workup with prolonged rhythm monitoring after any stroke to detect occult atrial fibrillation
Manage associated atrial arrhythmias as they arise
Follow up with echocardiography to characterise the aneurysm and any accompanying interatrial shunt
Coordinate care between cardiology and stroke neurology where paradoxical embolism has occurred
